title: Insecto and AI for Insect Farming
headline: Camera and sensor units for insect farms in the UK and Africa, and the joint PhD that used their data for machine-vision automation and digital-twin yield forecasting
photoAlt: Insect habitat seen from above with each insect detected and boxed by the machine-vision model
subtitle: Camera and sensor units that watch insect habitats around the clock, and the PhD that used their data to automate insect farming with machine vision
need: Insects are a promising source of protein for livestock feed, but farming them at scale is hard. Yields vary with temperature, humidity, light and feed, disease spreads quickly in dense colonies, and checking fertility, sex ratio and health by eye is slow and inconsistent.

Bristol Robotics Lab was running a project to help small-scale insect farmers in Africa. It needed low-cost units that could monitor many habitats at once, capture images at regular intervals and send the data to the cloud for analysis.
role: SciFlair designed and built the Insecto units: hardware, enclosure, firmware and cloud connection. We then co-funded and co-supervised a PhD with the University of the West of England that used the units and their data to research automated insect farming.
built: Insecto units: a high-resolution camera and environmental sensors in a compact, wall-mounted enclosure, one per habitat
Monitoring and remote control of temperature, humidity, airflow, moisture and light for each habitat
Images captured at set intervals and sent with the sensor data to a cloud server, so many experiments can run in parallel
Machine-vision models (object detection and segmentation) that find and count insects, tell larvae, pupae and adults apart, and flag signs of disease from colour, movement and body shape
A ground-truth image and sensor dataset from working insect habitats
A digital-twin predictor that forecasts yield from species, feed and environment, so farm settings can be adjusted for a consistent harvest

delivery.title: Concept
delivery.text: Defined the stakeholder needs with Bristol Robotics Lab: low cost, modular, remote monitoring of many habitats, suitable for small farms.

delivery.title: Design and build
delivery.text: Designed the unit and its enclosure in CAD, then built and tested a batch of units in our lab in 2021.

delivery.title: Deployment
delivery.text: Units went into use in the UK and in Africa, collecting images and environmental data from live insect habitats.

delivery.title: Research
delivery.text: The joint PhD used the units and their data to train and validate machine-vision models and build the yield predictor, repeating experiments and checking results against published work.

delivery.title: Completion
delivery.text: The PhD completed and the researcher graduated in 2026.

nextGen.title: Next: A Commercial Demonstrator
nextGen.text: We are looking for partners and funders to build a commercial demonstrator: modular, decentralised insect farming in which small farmers run breeding or rearing units guided by machine vision.
